Hongkong, Saturday, October 9, 1926.
A SATURDAY CAUSERIE.

This week has seen continued assurances on the part of Canton as to the capacity of the officials to deal effectively with the pickets and enable normal trade relations to be resumed between Hong Kong and Canton as from tomorrow. It is to be hoped that their confidence is justified and that the declarations of other leaders in Canton that the pickets will undergo reorganisation and will continue their activities in intensified form are unauthorised outbursts unfounded in fact and uttered merely with the object of fulfilling that almost sacred necessity in China for "saving face" even if it be at the expense of all truth and reason.

That there are directors of obstructive tactics in Canton who do not see in recent developments in Canton the end to their regime is apparent from the fact that there have been sent to Hong Kong quite recently agitators who are charged with the duty of introducing their insidious doctrines into certain of the Chinese schools here—doctrines which are far from introducing that element of peace and harmony in the relations between Hong Kong and Canton that the new era is said to be ushering in Mr. Eugene Chen and any other responsible officials who may be anxious for a settlement in order that a trial may be given to the proposed institution of taxes—to be paid by the Southern Chinese people themselves—have an unenviable task if the policy of the several factions in Canton is as opposed as it would appear from recent declarations.

It is extremely doubtful if the Government's intention, ascertained this week, to rebuild the Government Civil Hospital on a site adjoining the present will commend itself to the general public and it is probable—if provision for the work of rebuilding is included in the estimates for next year—that Unofficial members will have something to say on the matter at the Budget debate. With negotiations proceeding with regard to hospital accommodation on the Peak, the outcome of which will be either that the present Peak Hospital will be very much enlarged and improved or that work will be put in hand on the War Memorial Nursing Home, there would appear to be sufficient accommodation for Europeans, at any rate, on the Peak or at the French Hospital. Would the need be such, then, that the Government would be justified in putting in hand a scheme which it is stated will cost something like three million dollars?

There are many who think that, with further accommodation for patients provided on the Peak, the putting in hand of internal improvements at the G.C.H. and its reservation, with the exception of an emergency ward, as a hospital for the Chinese would solve the problem of hospital accommodation and that there is not the need for the expensive rebuilding which the Government contemplates. The present policy of the Government is, however, to include in the proposed new Hospital, accommodation enlarged for Europeans as well as in other respects. Having regard to this fact, there is logic in the argument that if Europeans are to be accommodated on a larger scale their needs should also be considered in regard to the site of the Hospital. The present site may be conveniently situated for the poorer Chinese residents who form the bulk of the patients but it is far from ensuring the seclusion from noise which, in the case of patients not accustomed to the sounds attendant on all Chinese neighbourhoods, may affect very adversely their condition. Either the Government should devote the Hospital exclusively to Chinese, in which case such extensive rebuilding would not be needed, or else remove the site of the Hospital to a more suitable neighbourhood.

MOTOR 'BUSES, LABELS, KOWLOON.

Sir,—The "Star" Ferry runs between Hong Kong and Kowloon. The Hong Kong terminus is labelled "Kowloon Ferry" and the Kowloon terminus is labelled "Hong Kong Ferry." This, one gather's, is correct. Why therefore are all the buses running in Kowloon labelled "to Kowloon Ferry"?

Yours, etc.,
Peeping Tom.
Hong Kong, Oct. 9.
REPUBLIC ANNIVERSARY.

Sir,—It is truly a sign of the times to find an individual in the person of your correspondent "Well-Wisher" in rising to the occasion as to prompt celebration of the Anniversary of the Chinese Republic by the two Chinese Legislative Councillors as representatives here of the Chinese people. I heartily applaud for the sentimental manner in which "Well-Wisher's" letter was written and I fully concur with "Well-Wisher's" hope that meetings between the East and West would be the means of drawing intimately together the bonds that unite these two friendly nations in terms of the utmost cordiality.
"Well-Wisher," whocover he may be, has a keen sense of that patriotic spirit which forms a great asset to a nation and his excellent example has multiple values.
Yours, etc.
“THE SHIP.”
ENGINEERS' INSTITUTE PAPERS.
SESSION'S PROGRAMME
The literary council of the Institution of Engineers and Shipbuilders of Hong Kong is making a strenuous effort to revive a very important feature, viz., the reading of technical papers.

Four such have been definitely promised for the coming session.
On October 22, Mr. J. S. Gillingham, M.I.N.A., M.B.E., of the Royal Corps of Naval Constructors, is to read a more or less historical paper on "The Ship." By such a distinguished personage, it should merit a large and enthusiastic audience.
During November, Mr. Chesterton (local representative of "Marconis") and Mr. G. F. Taylor (the well-known Hong Kong expert and enthusiast) will lecture and demonstrate on wireless and radio work and continue in December. Details will be announced later. Mr. Hevey (of the Gas Co.) will read a paper in January, probably dealing with the manufacture, distribution and use of gas.
It is hoped to get up another paper for February.
Mr. J. Ormiston, (President and convener of the literary council) is to be congratulated on his organising efforts. The "China Mail" hopes that he will meet with further success.

Friends (including ladies) are invited. Those interested in any way are strongly recommended to attend. Institute "papers" in the past have been noteworthy events in the Hong Kong winter season and it is to be hoped that members will come forward as often as possible.
NEW CHINESE GRAMMAR

A new Chinese grammar, with copious illustrations and quotations from the best works, styled ("A Grammar of the Chinese Language"), has been published by the Chi Hua Book Room, No. 31F (2nd floor), Wyndham Street, Hong Kong.
The author' Mr. Hu Kun-chi, formerly senior Anglo-Chinese master at the Diocesan Boys' School, has endeavoured to exhibit the structure of the Chinese language in a clear and logical manner.
The book will prove useful to non-Chinese students of the language as well as to the Chinese and should prove a decided acquisition to libraries.
THE E.A.S.M.A.
YEAR OF VARIED ACTIVITIES.

The annual report of the Ex-Active Service Men's Association Committee for the past year has just been issued. It says in part: "It is with the keenest regret that your Committee have to record the death of the Hon. Sir Paul Chater. In him the Colony has lost a citizen to whom it owes much and your Association a patron and friend to whom is due its actual existence to-day."

During the year 75 new members joined the Association and 13 ceased to be members through death, resignation and other reasons. Your Committee sincerely regret to report the deaths of the following six members: J. W. Lee, G. S. Falkner, J. M. Anderson, A. R. P. Davies, C. H. Lyson, and A. Reid.
Owing to the departure on leave in April, 1926, of your Hon. Secretary, Mr. T. N. MacReynolds, Mr.

T. A. Barry was co-opted on to the Committee to act until his return as Hon. Secretary. Owing to business reasons, however, he was unable to accept office, and Mr. R. J. Hunt was elected to fill the vacancy, which he has done in a particularly able manner.
Messrs. R. S. W. Paterson and R. S. Moore resigned from the Committee in May, 1926, and Messrs. W. S. Dixon and S. A. Roberts were co-opted in their places.
Finance.
RAILWAY STRIKE

[From Our Own Correspondent.]
Pakkal, Kongmoon, Oct. 5.
To maintain communication while the employees are on strike for better pay, the garrison commander of the Five Districts has taken over control of the Sunning Railway and the service has been resumed, at least, temporarily.
The military are paying the employees for the time being.
Your Committee have to report a loss of $132.95 on the year's Profit and Loss Account as against a loss last year of $1,430.65, and this is in spite of a decrease in Bar profits of over a thousand dollars. Subscriptions for this year amount to $1,250 as against $470 last year, the difference being accounted for by the receipt of a large number of Subscriptions for past years.

With regard to the Balance Sheet, cash at Bank and in hand amounts to a satisfactory figure of $706.66. In past years the disfiguring item in our Balance Sheet has been bad debts. This year it has been decided, on the advice of your Auditors, to write off all the bad and doubtful debts incurred prior to August 31, 1925 against Reserve Account, which is reduced in consequence by the very large figure of $3,119.96.

The actual bad debts incurred this year only amount to $837.60 of which $185.15 are in respect of deceased members' accounts, and it has never been the practice to collect outstanding accounts in such cases. To your Acting Honorary Secretary is due the credit for keeping down this item, and it is to be hoped that in the future members will co-operate cheerfully in the policy of ensuring prompt monthly settlements.

It is to be regretted that a further sum of $231.81 has had to be written off agk_nst the year's Profit and Loss Account owing to the failure of the clerk to carry forward certain items in the Club's monthly accounts.

There was only an average attendance at the local Cenotaph Ceremony. A wreath from the Association was placed on the Cenotaph in London by Messrs. L. W. Cressey and W. Hill, who were on leave from the Colony.
Thanks are due to Messrs. S. C. Feltham, R. C. Wilson, R. J. Hunt and H. H. Rose for special work in connection with the organisation of the annual dinner.

There have been very few applications for relief during the year, which is somewhat surprising in view of the general trade and commercial depression. The total amount expended was $462.57 although only $142.90 appears in the Balance Sheet. This is due to the fact that $283.87 was refunded, which is a pleasing indication that the applicants were genuinely seeking relief and not charity.

BANDIT TERRORS.
MACHINE-GUN FIRE ON A SHOP.

[From Our Own Correspondent.]
Pakka: Kongmoon Oct. 6
Famous now for its achievements against bandits, the 13th division of the Nationalist Army has been transferred to Shekki where outlaws are active.

Since the withdrawal of part of the garrisons for Canton's war against the north, robbers have been coming out into the open.
Only recently the 18th division shot a good many alleged pirate chieftains. Major-Gen. Chu King-tong and Brig.-Gen. Chan Cheung-po are the heroes of this part of the delta.
At Kowkong, one gang brought up a machine-gun in daylight and opened fire at point blank range into a shop which had refused to pay blackmail.
Hardly an inmate escaped. Everybody from master down to the lowest foki was either killed or wounded.
Since this incident, over a hundred shopkeepers in the same district have received similar threatening demands.
The military are co-operating with the volunteer militia in keeping order.

In the latter case the trophy was allocated to a Service Race.

Indoors, an experiment was made in the form of a Bridge Drive, but the response was poor. This unfortunately was also the case with one or two informal entertainments given by Naval Concert parties in the Club Rooms. The billiard table continues to be well patronised and a marker has now been engaged who cannot only mark but also play a very fair game.

The Beach at Stonecutters' Island was opened on May 22, 1926. In the middle of July the midweek trips were discontinued, owing to lack of support, an insufficient number of members being able for business reasons to get away during the week.

The running of the Beach resulted in a loss of $1,416.77 as against $2,294.61 last year. The considerable difference in these figures is due to the fact that in this year's accounts; moneys directly received from the Beach have been credited to the Beach Account. By this method the actual loss incurred is respect of the Beach is shown for the first time.

The Annual Sweepstake on the Hong Kong Derby was won by Messrs. S. A. Roberts and J. A. Gordon Leask jointly. The first prize amounted to $8,100.03, and the Association Funds benefited to the extent of $390.62, net profit.
